acts.title: How much is actually left
text: There are perhaps four days of my childhood I can ___ in any detail at all.
One of them I remember so ___ that I could draw the room.
Two more I remember only ___ — a shape, a colour, somebody laughing.
The fourth has ___ so far that I am no longer sure whether it is mine or my sister’s.
Of the year we moved house I have almost no ___ , which everybody in the family finds strange.

items.q: Although I was only two, I can ___ it vividly.

acts.title: Text A · The day the war ended
text: My clearest childhood memory is the day the Second World War ended. It was May 1945, so I must have been four.

I do not remember deciding to go anywhere. What I remember is being on a train to London, a hundred miles away, which on a steam train took most of the day, and then standing in front of Buckingham Palace.

The royal family were on the balcony. Everybody around us was cheering, and I can still hear how loud it was. My father let me sit on his shoulders so that I could see, and I remember trying not to hold on to his hair.
What I recall most clearly is a disappointment. The queen was wearing pale blue, which was right. Princess Elizabeth was wearing a brown army uniform, and I had expected her to look like a princess.
I have absolutely no recollection of how we got home.

items.q: What is the writer describing?
o: Her clearest childhood memory, from May 1945

items.q: What disappointed her?
o: Princess Elizabeth was in army uniform, not a princess’s dress

acts.title: Text B · The first and last horse
text: I will never forget going horse riding for the first — and last — time, at about ten, on a school activity holiday.
All the other children were excited. I pretended to be excited, and I remember feeling nervous, because I had never done it and was slightly frightened of horses.

Everything was fine while the horse was walking. When it started to trot I felt completely out of control. I did not expect it to run so fast. I tried to get it to slow down; it kept on running. In my panic I forgot to follow the teacher’s instructions.

To make matters worse, my helmet had slipped down over my eyes, so I could not see a thing. That is the part I remember most clearly — not being able to see. I did not dare to take my hands off the reins.
So I decided to do something very silly. I made myself fall off. I do not remember whether I was injured. My pride certainly was.

items.s: The writer had ridden a horse before.
He pretended to be excited like the other children.
He remembered the teacher’s instructions during the panic.
His helmet slipped and blocked his view.
He fell off the horse deliberately.
He is certain he was not injured.

acts.title: Look again at the two texts
text: I do not remember deciding to go anywhere.
In my panic I forgot to follow the teacher’s instructions.
I remember feeling nervous.
I tried to get it to slow down.
I did not dare to take my hands off the reins.
My father let me sit on his shoulders.

items.q: “I do not remember deciding to go.” What does remember + -ing mean?
o: The deciding happened first; the remembering came after

items.q: “I forgot to follow the instructions.” What actually happened?
o: He followed them and forgot afterwards

items.q: “I tried to get it to slow down.” What does try + infinitive mean here?
o: He experimented to see what would happen

items.q: “My father let me sit…” — what follows let?
o: A person, then a bare infinitive

acts.title: -ing or to: three groups, and one trap
rule: Some verbs take an -ing form, some take an infinitive, and a few take either with different meanings. The first two groups are memory work. The third group is where B2 is actually tested, because both versions are grammatical and only one of them means what you intended.
points: enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest, keep on, imagine, deny, involve, practise.
decide, hope, expect, manage, refuse, offer, promise, agree, seem, dare.
want, ask, tell, expect, allow, get, force. I got the horse to slow down.
No to at all: make somebody do, let somebody do. But the passive restores it: he was made to leave.
remember, forget, stop, try, regret, go on. This is the group that matters.

acts.careful: “I stopped to smoke” and “I stopped smoking” are opposites. The first means you paused in order to have one; the second means you gave up. Both are correct English, so nothing will warn you.

write.q: Write about 180 words on one clear childhood memory and one that has almost gone. Use remember + -ing at least twice, remember or forget + to at least once, and one of make or let with a bare infinitive. Say what you cannot remember as well as what you can.
write.ph: The clearest thing I can recall…
plan: one small thing you recall exactly
what you cannot remember at all
write.model:
The clearest thing I can recall from before school is my grandmother’s kitchen at five in the morning, which means it must have been a baking day.

I remember standing on a chair she had put there for me, and I remember being allowed to press the dough with one finger and told not to do it twice. She let me carry one tray to the window, and I have never since been trusted with anything so carefully.

What I recall exactly is the smell of the wet flour on my hands, which is a strange thing for a memory to keep.

The faded one is the funeral, four years later. I vaguely remember a room full of coats. I remember forgetting to say something I had been told to say, and being embarrassed about it for a week.

Of the journey home I have no recollection whatsoever, and I was old enough to have one.
